newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania president confronts PM on security forces.
newsitem.headline: Albania president confronts PM on security forces.

text.p: Confrontation over control of Albania's security forces burst into the open on Wednesday between President Sali Berisha and the Socialists on course to defeat his Democratic Party in general elections.

The Balkan country's interim government, led by a Socialist, accused Berisha of blocking its attempts to establish control over the ministry -- a key institution in quelling months of country-wide rebellion.

Government spokesman Vladimir Prela said Berisha had tried overnight to block the government's decision to put a Socialist appointee in charge of interior ministry operations. The interior minister and his deputy left Albania after the size of the Socialist election win became apparent.

Armed groups confronted each other into the early hours of the morning around Tirana's central Skanderbeg Square, but it was impossible to identify which institutions they represented. No shots were fired and the groups later dispersed.
Prela said unidentified troops had also surrounded the prime minister's office for a time during the night.
"Berisha was extremely nervous," he told reporters. "It took several hours of frantic telephone calls to calm matters down. The ministry is completely under the control of the government."

Although counting is still proceeding, Berisha conceded his Democrats had been beaten into opposition less than 24 hours after the polls closed. But he has said nothing about whether he intends to step down.
The Socialists have called the first authorised rally for Wednesday evening, between the two rounds of the election.

Berisha's spokeswoman, Linda Ihsani, said the problem was rooted in a March agreement setting up the multi-party government and staging last Sunday's election giving the interior ministry to a Democratic Party appointee.
"The minister is gone and must be replaced," she said by telephone. "We have an agreement which says the minister must be from the Democratic Party. This is a normal procedure."
Control of the interior ministry is viewed as a key step in stamping the authority of any government on what was one of Europe's most repressive communist regimes until 1990.
It is also critical to putting an end to the violence which has killed more than 1,500 people this year.
Socialist leader Fatos Nano told reporters on Tuesday that a Socialist Party member had put in charge of the ministry's operations after the minister, Belul Celo, had fled the country.
Police armoured vehicles then roared through central Tirana in a show of force.

Prela produced what he said was an order issued by Berisha for units of the elite republican guard to block all approach roads to Tirana as well as the central bank. Ihsani said she knew nothing about the document.
An order subsequently issued by Prime Minister Bashkim Fino effectively told troops to ignore the president's instructions.
Prela said the president was pressing for the appointment as interior minister of Azem Hajdari, one of his most loyal supporters within the Democratic Party.
"The prime minister insists that it is up to the government, not the president, to propose ministerial appointments," Prela said. "It is then up to the president to approve them."

Partial results in the slow count give the Socialists a big lead, though many contests will have to go to a run-off round on Sunday where no candidate won the 50 percent required for outright victory.

In a parallel referendum, voters appeared to have rejected restoration of the monarchy, according to partial returns, though Albania's self-proclaimed King Leka I said he had data showing the monarchy had been approved.
Several hundred monarchist supporters gathered in central Tirana on Wednesday and threatened to mass every day to denounce what they said was electoral fraud.
